scenario.childBackground: He is a 14-year-old Hispanic boy from a Mexican-American family, bilingual in English and some Spanish at home, and he often moves between his family’s expectations and his online social world. He lives with his mom and younger sister while his dad works long hours, and family time is mostly evenings and weekends when everyone is tired. Money is tight in a lower-middle-income apartment, so gaming is his main affordable hobby and his phone and headset are his primary way to socialize.
scenario.narrative:
After school, he logs onto his console in the living room and joins voice chat with people from a competitive gaming server. Over the last few weeks, he’s gotten especially close to one player who says they’re “basically the same age” and jokes about how adults “don’t get it.” They message him often—mostly about strategies, tournaments, and funny clips—but it’s also turned into long late-night conversations that feel personal in a way his real-life friends don’t.

One night, his mom calls from the kitchen asking who he’s talking to and reminds him about homework. He mutes his mic, annoyed and embarrassed, and types to his friend that his mom is “always on me.” The friend replies that parents always ruin things and suggests they keep their chats and gaming sessions “just between us,” saying it’s normal to have a friendship space without “parental interference.” They point out that if his mom knew how much they talk, she’d probably start asking questions or taking away his headset, so it’s easier if he doesn’t mention the friend at all.

He feels a mix of excitement and pressure—like being invited into a special circle—and also a little nervous that he’s doing something he’d have to explain. Still, he tells himself it’s harmless because they’re “just gaming” and his mom doesn’t understand online friends anyway. He starts thinking about how to make sure no one overhears, like lowering his voice when he’s on mic and quickly switching screens when someone walks by, and he keeps the friend’s username out of family conversations.
